title: Efficient electroreduction of CO2 to C2-C3 products on Cu/Cu2O@N-doped graphene
abstract: CO2 is the main gas that causes the greenhouse effect, so electrochemical reduction of CO2 can be regarded as a solution to alleviate the climate crisis. In this study, a simple metal–organic frameworks (MOFs)-derivatized strategy was adopted to prepare electrocatalyst, where MOF-199 and N-doped graphene (NG), as precursors, were electroreduced to obtain Cu/Cu2O@N-doped graphene (Cu/Cu2O@NG) materials for efficient CO2 electroreduction to produce C2-C3 products (ethylene, ethanol and n-propanol). A series of Cu/Cu2O@NG materials, especially Cu/Cu2O@NG-2 with a Faraday efficiency of 56 % and corresponding current density of 19.0 mA/cm2 for C2-C3 products, showed a considerably better catalytic performance compared with the MOF-199-derived Cu/ Cu2O material. This good performance was mainly attributed to the synergistic effect between the evenly dispersed Cu/Cu2O and NG, leading to good CO2 adsorption capacity, rapid mass transfer and abundant active sites.

Efficient electroreduction of CO2 to C2-C3 products on Cu/ Cu2O@N-doped graphene
Wen-Ya Zhi 1, Yu-Ting Liu 1, Si-Li Shan, Cheng-Jie Jiang, Huan Wang *, Jia-Xing Lu * Shanghai Key Laboratory of Green Chemistry and Chemical Processes, School of Chemistry and Molecular Engineering, East China Normal University, Shanghai, 200062, China
A R T I C L E I N F O
Keywords: Cu/Cu2O particles Metal–organic frameworks C2-C3 products CO2RR Catalytic performance
A B S T R A C T
CO2 is the main gas that causes the greenhouse effect, so electrochemical reduction of CO2 can be regarded as a solution to alleviate the climate crisis. In this study, a simple metal–organic frameworks (MOFs)-derivatized strategy was adopted to prepare electrocatalyst, where MOF-199 and N-doped graphene (NG), as precursors, were electroreduced to obtain Cu/Cu2O@N-doped graphene (Cu/Cu2O@NG) materials for efficient CO2 electroreduction to produce C2-C3 products (ethylene, ethanol and n-propanol). A series of Cu/Cu2O@NG materials, especially Cu/Cu2O@NG-2 with a Faraday efficiency of 56 % and corresponding current density of 19.0 mA/cm2 for C2-C3 products, showed a considerably better catalytic performance compared with the MOF-199-derived Cu/ Cu2O material. This good performance was mainly attributed to the synergistic effect between the evenly dispersed Cu/Cu2O and NG, leading to good CO2 adsorption capacity, rapid mass transfer and abundant active sites.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
CO2 is the main gas causing the greenhouse effect; thus, electroreduction of CO2 (CO2RR) can not only effectively alleviate the greenhouse effect [1–3], but also turn waste into various compounds with commercial application value, such as ethanol, ethylene, acetate and n-propanol (C2-C3 products) [4,5]. Therefore, studies should focus on the CO2RR to prepare C2-C3 compounds.
Copper-based catalysts have attracted wide attention [6–8] because of their low cost and high selectivity for the formation of C2 products [9–11], especially Cu/Cu2O catalysts with a high selectivity for C2 products. For example, Shang et al. [12] synthesised a Cu/Cu2O catalyst with a high Faraday efficiency (FE) of 50 % for C2 products (ethylene and ethanol).
Nitrogen-doped graphene (NG) is widely used in electrocatalysis owing to its high surface area and excellent electrical conductivity [13–15]. Ning et al. [16] reported that the introduction of NG facilitated the dispersion of Cu2O nanoparticles and showed dual catalytic activity. Yuan et al. [17] reported that Cu nanoparticles decorated on pyridoxine-modified graphene oxide sheets exhibited a high FE for ethanol (56.3 %).
Metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) are crystalline materials with a periodic network structure and are widely used in many fields [18–20]. However, given their low stability during electrolysis [21], MOFs are recommended to use as precursors to derive new materials, such as metals, metal oxides and nanoparticle@carbon [22–24], rather than as direct catalysts for CO2RR. Kim et al. [25] reported that MOF-74-derived copper particles benefited methane production (FE > 50 %). Zhao et al. [26] synthesised an oxide-derived Cu/C catalyst from MOF with a high FE of 71.2 % for ethanol and methanol.
Based on these studies, a simple MOF derivative strategy was proposed in this work. Cu-MOF and NG, as precursors, were electroreduced to obtain a new electrocatalyst for efficient CO2RR into C2-C3 products. MOF-199 possessed a regular structure, which would promote the production of Cu/Cu2O particles with uniform size. NG, which acted as supports, could disperse Cu/Cu2O particles and inhibit their agglomeration. Therefore, we prepared Cu/Cu2O@NG materials (Scheme 1), in which uniform Cu/Cu2O particles were distributed evenly on NG, which has a positively impact on CO2RR.

sections.heading: 2.1. Chemical reagents
sections.text: Copper (II) nitrate trihydrate (Cu(NO3)2•3H2O), ethanol (99.9 %) and potassium iodide (KI) were purchased from Sinopharm Chemical Reagent Co., Ltd. Nafion®-117 solution was purchased from Beijing Warwick. 1,3,5-benzenetricarboxylic acid (H3BTC, > 98.0 %) was purchased from Shanghai Maclean Biochemical Technology Co., Ltd. Ndoped graphene (NG) was purchased from Xianfeng Nano. All reagents were used without further purification.

sections.heading: 2.2. Material characterizations
sections.text: Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) images were obtained on a Hitachi S-4800 field-emission scanning electron microscope. Transmission electron microscopy (TEM), high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM) and energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) elemental mapping measurements were conducted on a high-resolution transmission electron microscope (Hitachi JEM-2100 F). X-ray diffraction (XRD) studies were performed on an Ultima IV X-ray powder diffractometer equipped with Cu Kα radiation (k =1.5406 Å). X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) analysis was performed on a Thermo Scientific ESCA Lab 250Xi equipped with 200 W monochromatic Al Kα radiation. The element content were quantified by Inductively Coupled Plasma Atomic Emission Spectrometry (ICP-AES) on a Thermo IRIS Intrepid II XSP atomic emission spectrometer.

sections.heading: 2.3. Material synthesis
sections.text:
MOF-199 was synthesised in accordance with the method described in the literature [27]. A Cu (NO3)2•3H2O aqueous solution (7.5 mL, 0.4 M) was added to a H3BTC ethanol solution (7.5 mL, 0.13 M) and stirred for 30 min. The mixture was placed in an oven at 120 ◦C for 24 h. After cooling to room temperature, the material was washed thrice with ethanol and dried at 85 ◦C under vacuum for 12 h to obtain MOF-199.
A simple MOF-derivatised strategy was adopted to obtain Cu/ Cu2O@NG materials, in which MOF-199 was electroreduced to Cu/ Cu2O particles on NG. All electrochemical experiments were performed using a CHI 660D electrochemical station (Shanghai Chenhua Instrument Co., Ltd.). 0.2 M KI aqueous solution was used as the electrolyte solution in all experiments. Typically, 10 mg mixture of MOF-199 and NG (mass ratio = 4:1) were dispersed uniformly in a solution containing 30 μL Nafion® 117 and 60 μL water by ultrasonication for 0.5 h. The
suspension of MOF-199 and NG was coated on a carbon paper (area= 1.77 cm2), which was named MOF-199-NG/carbon paper. Then, Cu/ Cu2O@NG-2 was obtained by chronoamperometry at -1.9 V versus reversible hydrogen electrode (vs. RHE) for 5 min by using the MOF199-NG/carbon paper as the working electrode, a platinum mesh as the counter electrode and a saturated calomel electrode (SCE) as the reference electrode. The potential in all the text was referred to RHE and determined using the following equation: E (vs. RHE) = E (vs. SCE) + 0.241 + 0.0591 × pH. The pH of the CO2-saturated KI solution (0.2 M) was 5.17. The synthetic process of Cu/Cu2O@NG-1 and Cu/Cu2O@NG3 was similar to the above procedure, except for the changes in the mass ratios of MOF-199 and NG (9:1, 7:3). Cu/Cu2O was also prepared with the same procedure, except that only MOF-199 was used as precursors.

sections.heading: 2.4. Electrochemical measurements
sections.text:
The preparation of the working electrode used in the linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) experiments was described as followed. 1 mg of Cu/ Cu2O@NG was dispersed uniformly in 45 μL of Nafion®117 solution by ultrasonication for 0.5 h. Then 1 μL of the suspension of Cu/Cu2O@NG was coated on a glassy carbon electrode (r =1 mm).
The LSV tests were carried out in a single compartment cell, which was composed of a glassy carbon electrode coating material as the working electrode, a platinum mesh as the counter electrode and an SCE as the reference electrode, in the range of − 1.0 to − 2.1 V vs. RHE under N2 and CO2 atmosphere, respectively.

sections.heading: 2.5. Electroreduction of CO2
sections.text:
The preparation of the working electrode used in the electrolysis experiments was described as followed. 2 mg of Cu/Cu2O@NG catalyst was dispersed uniformly in a solution containing 20 μL of Nafion®117 and 40 μL of water by ultrasonication for 0.5 h. The suspension of Cu/ Cu2O@NG catalyst was coated on a carbon paper (area = 1.77 cm2). The loading of Cu/Cu2O@NG catalyst was 1.1 mg/cm2. The electrolysis experiments were conducted at 25 ◦C in a gas diffusion electrode cell, which was composed of a carbon paper coating Cu/Cu2O@NG catalyst as the working electrode, a platinum mesh as the counter electrode and an SCE as the reference electrode. 0.2 M KI aqueous solution was selected as the electrolyte.
All working electrodes were freshly prepared before each experiment. Prior to testing, high-purity CO2 (99.995 %) was bubbled through the catholyte for 30 min, and CO2 was delivered to the electrolysis cell at a flow rate of 10 sccm during electrolysis. The gaseous products were

collected and analysed by a gas chromatograph (Agilent, GC 7890) equipped with PLOT/Q column (30 m × 0.32 mm × 0.2 μm, Agilent), a thermal conductivity detector (TCD) and a flame ionization detector (FID). High-purity argon was worked as carrier gas. TCD was used to detect H2 and CO, while FID was used to detect CH4 and C2H4.The liquid products were detected by a gas chromatograph (Shimadzu, GC-2014C) equipped with an FID, HP-PLOT/Q column (30 m × 0.32 mm × 0.2 μm, Agilent) and headspace injection. High-purity N2 was worked as carrier gas. The FE of products were evaluated according to Eq. (1):
FE = nZF/Q × 100 % (1)
where n is the amount of substance of the product, Z is the theoretical number of exchanged electrons to form the products (the values are 2, 2, 8, 12, 12 and 18 corresponding to CO, H2, CH4, C2H4, C2H5OH and npropanol, respectively), F is the Faradaic constant (96485 C/mol), and Q is the total charge applied in the electrolysis process.

sections.heading: 3. Results and discussion
sections.text:
The X-ray diffraction (XRD) pattern of synthesized MOF-199 (Fig. 1a) was consistent with the simulated curve, indicating that MOF-199 was successfully prepared. After electroreduction, the diffraction peaks of MOF-199 disappeared in the XRD patterns of Cu/ Cu2O and Cu/Cu2O@NG (Fig. 1b). Diffraction peaks at 29.6◦, 36.4◦, 42.4◦, 61.3◦, 73.2◦ and 77.7◦ are corresponding to (110), (111), (200), (220), (311) and (222) crystal planes of Cu2O (JCPDS PDF#74-1230), respectively. The peaks at 43.5◦, 50.7◦ and 74.7◦ are indexed to the (111), (200) and (220) crystal planes of Cu (JCPDS PDF#85-1326), respectively. These results demonstrated that Cu and Cu2O were derived from MOF-199. The peak at 26.7◦ is belong to carbon paper (Fig. S1). The peak intensity of metal was excessively large, whereas that of NG was unremarkable at 24◦ in the XRD patterns of Cu/Cu2O@NG.
The surface morphology was characterized by Scanning electron microscopy (SEM). The morphology of NG is wrinkled (Fig. 2a), whereas MOF-199 shows a regular octahedron (Fig. 2b), which is consistent with results reported in the literature [28]. The SEM image of Cu/Cu2O (Fig. 2c) showed the particles with an average particle size of 60 nm. However, serious agglomeration of clusters occurred. As shown in the SEM images of Cu/Cu2O@NG (Figs. 2d and S2), after adding NG, the agglomeration of nanoparticles is obviously alleviated. Cu/Cu2O particles are distributed on NG one by one, and the particle size is reduced to ca 25 nm. Hence, NG played an important role in inhibiting the agglomeration of Cu/Cu2O particles, reducing their particle size and synthesizing even dispersed Cu/Cu2O particles, which can improve the performance of catalysts. Additional details were provided in the following text.
Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) was performed to determine the distribution of Cu and Cu2O in Cu/Cu2O@NG-2. As shown in the TEM image of Cu/Cu2O@NG-2 (Fig. 3), particles with a size of
approximately 22 nm were uniformly dispersed on the yarn-like substance, consistent with the results of SEM. In contrast, Cu/Cu2O accumulated severely when no NG was added (Fig. S3). The energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) element mapping of Cu/Cu2O@NG-2 (Fig. S4, where the pink and red dots represented the distributions of carbon and Cu, respectively) showed that the nanoparticles were composed of Cu, and the yarn-like substances were mainly composed of C, which were NG, consistent with the previous SEM results. Cu and Cu2O phases were observed in the high resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM) image of Cu/Cu2O@NG-2. As shown in lattice images (Fig. 3b), the fringes with spacings of 0.246 and 0.213 nm, marked by the red lines, corresponded to Cu2O (111) and (200) crystal planes, respectively. The fringe with a spacing of 0.208 nm marked by a blue line was Cu (111) crystal plane. These findings indicated that the nanoparticles were composed of Cu2O (111 and 200 crystal planes) and Cu (111 crystal plane), consistent with the XRD results. These results also revealed that the Cu and Cu2O particles of Cu/Cu2O@NG were prepared by removing organic components from the MOF-199 skeleton during electrochemical reduction. By increasing the mass ratio of NG, the copper content in the samples gradually decreased from 22.5 % to 13.5 % (Table S1), determined by inductively coupled plasma atomic emission spectrometry (ICP-AES).
The Cu/Cu2O@NG-2 was characterised by X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) to analyse its element valences. The XPS diagram of Cu/Cu2O@NG-2 Cu 2p (Fig. 4a) presented Cu2+ at 934.2 eV, whereas no Cu2+ detected on the HRTEM and XRD. This difference may be due to the particle size of Cu/Cu2O was considerably small that the surface was easily partially oxidised; thus, a small amount of Cu2+ was detected by XPS, as reported in the literature [29]. Determining whether the peak at 932.4 eV was Cu or Cu2O was difficult due to the similar binding energies of both compounds [30]. Thus, the LMM Auger characterisation of Cu (Fig. 4b) was conducted, in which the peaks at around 568.06 eV, 569.01 eV, and 572.74 eV are assigned to Cu◦, Cu+, and Cu2+ respectively. The result indicated that Cu/Cu2O@NG-2 contained Cu and Cu2O. As shown in the XPS diagram of N1 s (Fig. 4c), the peak at 398.3 eV was pyridinic nitrogen, whereas that at 399.4 eV was pyrrolic nitrogen.
LSV tests were conducted to measure the electrochemical activity of Cu/Cu2O@NG materials. Fig. 5a demonstrates LSV curves of Cu/ Cu2O@NG-2 obtained under N2 and CO2 atmospheres from − 0.4 to − 2.1 V vs. RHE. The current density on Cu/Cu2O@NG-2 under CO2 atmosphere was significantly higher than that under N2 atmosphere from − 1.0 to − 2.1 V vs. RHE, indicating that Cu/Cu2O@NG-2 exhibited efficient electroreduction response to CO2. The LSV curves of Cu/Cu2O and Cu/Cu2O@NG materials under CO2 atmosphere (Fig. 5b) revealed that their current densities depended on the material types. Different types of materials showed varied responses to the electrochemical behaviour of CO2. From − 1.2 to − 2.1 V vs. RHE, the current density on Cu/Cu2O@NG-2 was significantly higher than those on the three other materials, indicating that the former showed the strongest

electrochemical response to CO2. LSV tests cannot provide conclusive evidence about the electro-
chemical reduction, so potentiostatic electrolysis was conducted to test further the electrocatalytic performances of materials. The Faraday efficiencies (FEs) for various catalysts at − 1.9 V vs. RHE was shown in Fig. 6a. The current densities for C2-C3 products and H2 on five catalysts at − 1.9 V vs. RHE were calculated to compare different catalysts’ catalytic performance, as listed in Table S2. In case of NG as catalysts, intense H2 evolution occurred during CO2RR, with a higher FE of 78 % and current density of 30.8 mA/cm2 for H2 than other catalysts. Under the same condition, Cu/Cu2O showed a FE of 45 % and current density of 13.5 mA/cm2 for H2. Meanwhile, the FEs and current densities for C2C3 products reached 31 % and 9.3 mA/cm2, respectively. When Cu/ Cu2O supported on NG, the FE and current densities for C2-C3 products were raised and those for H2 were descended, compared with Cu/Cu2O and NG material. Among Cu/Cu2O@NG materials, Cu/Cu2O@NG-2 showed the best electrocatalytic performance of CO2RR to C2-C3 products, with a FE up to 56 %, and current density as high as 19.0 mA/cm2. It can be seen from the SEM images that when the ratio of Cu/Cu2O to NG is high (Fig. S2a), Cu/Cu2O is not well dispersed, thereby reducing catalytic active sites. When the ratio of Cu/Cu2O to NG is low (Fig. S2b), although NG can effectively disperse Cu/Cu2O, it cannot provide a large
number of active sites because of the small amount of Cu. Therefore, it is obvious that Cu/Cu2O and NG in appropriate proportion play an important role in electroreduction of CO2 to C2-C3 products.
To explain why Cu/Cu2O@NG materials present good electrocatalytic performances of CO2RR, CO2 adsorption desorption and electrochemical impedance spectra tests were performed on Cu/Cu2O, NG and Cu/Cu2O@NG-2 materials. The capability of a material to adsorb CO2 was a prerequisite for its participation in a subsequent catalytic reduction reaction. Therefore, the CO2 adsorption capacity is important and relevant with the electrochemical performance of catalysts. Cu/ Cu2O@NG-2 exhibited a better CO2 adsorption capacity than Cu/Cu2O and NG materials, which is presented in Fig. S5. This result indicated that the combination of Cu/Cu2O and NG increased the CO2 adsorption capacity of Cu/Cu2O@NG-2, providing more CO2 for catalytic reactions and increasing the concentration of CO2 near the electrode surface. As shown in the Nyquist plots (Fig. S6), the semicircle radius of Cu/ Cu2O@NG-2 is smaller than those of NG and Cu/Cu2O, indicating that Cu/Cu2O@NG-2 could minimize the resistance for electron transfer, which greatly promotes the electron transfer during the electroreduction of CO2, insulting improved corresponding efficiency. Thus, we deduce that the high FEs and current densities for C2-C3 products on Cu/ Cu2O@NG materials can be attributed to the synergistic effect between

the evenly dispersed Cu/Cu2O and NG, which increased the concentration of CO2 near the electrode surface and enhanced mass transfer, facilitating the conversion of CO2 to CO* and further promoting C–C coupling reaction, leading to the formation of C2-C3 product [31].
Electrochemical active surface area (ECSA) tests were performed on Cu/Cu2O@NG materials to explain the highest catalytic activity of Cu/ Cu2O@NG-2, which are shown in Fig. 7. It can be clearly seen that the Cu/Cu2O@NG-2 exhibits the highest double layer capacitance of 286.62 μF/cm2, implying the biggest ECSA, among Cu/Cu2O@NG series materials. The lager ECSA, the more efficient exposure of active sites. Thus, the ECSA of Cu/Cu2O@NG-2 was larger than that of Cu/Cu2O@NG-1, indicating that the introduction of NG enabled exposure of active sites and thus improved electrocatalytic activity of Cu/Cu2O@NG-2. In addition, the ECSA of Cu/Cu2O@NG-2 was higher than that of Cu/
Cu2O@NG-3, suggesting that the excessive introduction of NG reduced active sites for CO2RR. These results were consistent with the electrochemical performance of the catalysts.
The FEs for different products were plotted to compare the selectivity of Cu/Cu2O@NG-2 at different potentials (Fig. 6b). The current densities for C2-C3 products and H2 on Cu/Cu2O@NG-2 at different potentials were calculated to evaluate the effect of electrolysis potential, listed in Table S3. The FEs and current densities for C2-C3 products first increased and then decreased, along with the negative shift of the electrolytic potential (from − 1.7 to − 2.1 V vs. RHE). The best catalytic effect was observed at − 1.9 V vs. RHE, showing the highest selectivity, the highest FE (56 %), and the highest corresponding current density (19.0 mA/ cm2) for C2-C3 products. A proper negative potential shift can provide substantial energy for the reaction, which in turn promotes CO2RR.

However, during the electrolysis process, CO2RR and H2 evolution reaction (HER) are a pair of competitive reactions. Too negative potential will significantly accelerate HER, thereby reducing the current density of CO2RR.
Potentiostatic electrolysis test was performed to obtain the current versus time curves of the electrolysis on Cu/Cu2O and Cu/Cu2O@NG-2 to investigate their catalytic stability (Figs. 8 and S7). Unlike Cu/Cu2O, Cu/Cu2O@NG-2 maintained a constant current with the increase in electrolysis time, suggesting its superior electrochemical stability. Moreover, there was no obvious decay in FE for C2-C3 products for Cu/ Cu2O@NG-2. This may be because of the Cu-N bond formed by the pyridine nitrogen contained in NG and copper, which benefitted the stabilisation of Cu/Cu2O particles, as reported in the literature [32–34]. Therefore, the synergistic effect between the evenly dispersed Cu/Cu2O and NG can also significantly enhance the electrochemical stability of Cu/Cu2O@NG-2.

sections.heading: 4. Conclusion
sections.text:
In this study, a series of Cu/Cu2O@NG materials was prepared by electrically reducing MOF-199 and NG with different mass ratios. Among Cu/Cu2O@NG materials, Cu/Cu2O@NG-2 showed the best electrocatalytic performance, with the highest FE (56 %) and corresponding current density (19.0 mA/cm2) for C2-C3 products at − 1.9 V vs. RHE. The introduction of NG facilitated the dispersion of Cu/Cu2O particles, inhibited their agglomeration, increased the catalytic active sites and enhanced the electrochemical stability of catalyst.
